intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for White built around the London System — a quiet, system-based opening rather than a sharp theoretical duel, where White develops the c1-bishop to f4 on move two, builds the solid d4/e3/c3 pyramid, and then plays the SAME comfortable plan against almost anything Black tries. Built the same way as the companion Sicilian, Queen's Gambit, Indian Defenses, English Opening, and King's Indian Attack encyclopedias: main plans, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp lines, typical mistakes, every line verified move-by-move for legality. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the London System (foundations — the Bf4 bishop, the pyramid, when the system applies and when it doesn't). Chapter 2: The London vs. the Classical ...d5 Setups. Chapter 3: The London vs. King's Indian and Modern Setups. Chapter 4: The London vs. Queen's Indian and ...b6 Setups. Chapter 5: The London vs. Slav and Semi-Slav Structures. Chapter 6: The London vs. ...e6, the Dutch, and Rare Setups. Chapter 7: The London Attacking Plans in Depth. Chapter 8: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Every line is completed to fifteen moves for each side with engine-verified top play, and every coach comment is preserved.

THE BISHOP STEPS ASIDE — and this is the detail that makes the whole plan sound. The bishop is beautifully placed on g3, but it also occupies the very square the g-pawn needs to reach. From h2 it keeps a strong diagonal while freeing g2-g4, so the coming advance can be supported by a pawn. Played at once, h5 would simply be captured: ...Bxh5 wins a pawn, because nothing defends the square. The timing matters just as much as the idea: with the queen still on d8 the same retreat would walk into ...Qxh4, so the moment is right only because Black has just committed the queen to c7.

SUPPORT FIRST, THEN ADVANCE. The pawn comes up to defend the h5-square before the thrust. Support, not speed, is what makes the h4-h5 plan work.
Black completes development, but the kingside is now the scene of the action.

THE THRUST. The pawn attacks the g6-bishop and forces a concession: the bishop cannot stay, because hxg6 wins it for a pawn, and it cannot go to f5 either, because gxf5 wins it there too. The pawn itself is safe on h5 because the g-pawn behind it defends the square.

Black gives up the bishop for White's d3-bishop — the only way to avoid losing it outright. White recaptures with the c-pawn next move, and the lesson of the study stands: a pawn storm is only as strong as the support behind it. The bishop had to leave g3 first, the g-pawn had to arrive before the thrust, and the whole plan needed one quiet, well-timed move to make it work.
